claim: Clostridium thermocellum is a cellulolytic thermophilic anaerobe considered a prime candidate for consolidated bioprocessing (CBP).
source: Clostridium thermocellum, a cellulolytic thermophilic anaerobe, is considered by many to be a prime candidate for the realization of consolidated bioprocessing (CBP) and is known as an industry standard for biofuel production.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established characteristic of C. thermocellum, drawing on established scientific knowledge about this organism.

claim: C. thermocellum is among the best biomass degraders identified to date in nature.
source: C. thermocellum is among the best biomass degraders identified to date in nature and produces ethanol as one of its main products.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on established knowledge about biomass degradation capabilities of various organisms.

claim: C. thermocellum produces ethanol as one of its main products.
source: C. thermocellum is among the best biomass degraders identified to date in nature and produces ethanol as one of its main products.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of C. thermocellum metabolism.

claim: Ethanol production using C. thermocellum is not economically viable.
source: Many studies have helped increase ethanol titers in this microbe; however, ethanol production using C. thermocellum is still not economically viable.
evidence: This is stated as a current limitation in the field, drawing on established knowledge about the economic status of C. thermocellum-based ethanol production.

claim: The main pathway for ethanol production in C. thermocellum involves the bifunctional aldehyde-alcohol dehydrogenase (AdhE).
source: The main pathway for ethanol production in C. thermocellum involves the bifunctional aldehyde-alcohol dehydrogenase (AdhE).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about C. thermocellum metabolism.

claim: A 3.28 Å cryo-EM structure of the C. thermocellum AdhE complex was obtained.
source: To better understand the function of the C. thermocellum AdhE, we used cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to obtain a 3.28 Å structure of the AdhE complex.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results from the study.

claim: The C. thermocellum AdhE structure provides insight into substrate channeling of the toxic intermediate acetaldehyde.
source: This high-resolution structure, in combination with molecular dynamics simulations, provides insight into the substrate channeling of the toxic intermediate acetaldehyde, indicates the potential role of C. thermocellum AdhE to regulate activity and cofactor pools, and establishes a basis for future engineering studies.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the structural data and MD simulations presented in the study.

claim: The containment strategy found in AdhE could be replicated in other systems where toxic intermediates need to be sequestered.
source: The containment strategy found in this enzyme offers a template that could be replicated in other systems where toxic intermediates need to be sequestered to increase the production of valuable biochemicals.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of the findings.

claim: Lignocellulosic biomass is an attractive substrate for sustainable production of second-generation biofuels.
source: Lignocellulosic biomass is one of the most attractive substrates for sustainable production of second-generation biofuels and other bioproducts (Ashokkumar et al., 2022; Biddy et al., 2016; Demain, 2009; Isikgor and Becer, 2015; Usmani et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Consolidated bioprocessing (CBP) is emerging as a promising process to reduce costs by combining biomass solubilization and fermentation in one step without added enzymes.
source: Consolidated bioprocessing (CBP) is emerging as a promising process to reduce costs by combining biomass solubilization and fermentation in one step without added enzymes (Fan, 2014; Lynd et al., 2002; Lynd et al., 1999; Lynd et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: C. thermocellum has been engineered to produce ethanol at high yield.
source: Due to its ability to quickly solubilize and utilize cellulose, Clostridium thermocellum is an ideal candidate organism for CBP and has previously been engineered to produce ethanol at high yield (Akinosho et al., 2014; Verbeke et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ethanol production using C. thermocellum is not yet economical due to limited titers.
source: However, ethanol production using C. thermocellum is not yet an economical process due to limited titers (Brown et al., 2011; Rani and Seenayya, 1999; Tian et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: AdhE is often modified in strains selected for alcohol tolerance and other selective pressures, indicating its crucial role in C. thermocellum metabolism.
source: The main pathway for ethanol production in C. thermocellum involves the bifunctional aldehyde-alcohol dehydrogenase (AdhE), a gene that is often modified in strains selected for alcohol tolerance and other selective pressures, indicating its crucial role in C. thermocellum metabolism (Tian et al., 2019; Lo et al., 2015; Olson et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: AdhE contains an aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) domain for the reduction of acetyl-CoA to acetaldehyde.
source: AdhE functions in the anaerobic fermentation pathway and contains two domains: an aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) domain for the reduction of acetyl-CoA to acetaldehyde and an alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) domain to reduce acetaldehyde to ethanol.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about AdhE structure and function.

claim: AdhE contains an alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) domain to reduce acetaldehyde to ethanol.
source: AdhE functions in the anaerobic fermentation pathway and contains two domains: an aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) domain for the reduction of acetyl-CoA to acetaldehyde and an alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) domain to reduce acetaldehyde to ethanol.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about AdhE structure and function.

claim: Both reduction processes in AdhE natively use NADH as a cofactor and are reversible in the presence of NAD+.
source: Both reduction processes natively use NADH as a cofactor and are reversible in the presence of NAD+ as a cofactor.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about AdhE enzymatic activity.

claim: AdhE forms large, filamentous helical ultrastructures termed spirosomes.
source: Structurally, AdhE is an intriguing protein as it forms large, filamentous helical ultrastructures termed spirosomes, that could be necessary for function (Kessler et al., 1992; Matayoshi and Oda, 1985).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In E. coli AdhE, spirosome formation seems vital for the forward reaction of acetyl-CoA to ethanol.
source: In the case of Echerichia coli AdhE, spirosome formation seems vital for the forward reaction of acetyl-CoA to ethanol, while the reverse reaction is not impacted by the disruption of the ultrastructures (Kim et al., 2019; Pony et al., 2020; Espinosa et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The reverse reaction in E. coli AdhE is not impacted by the disruption of the spirosome ultrastructures.
source: In the case of Echerichia coli AdhE, spirosome formation seems vital for the forward reaction of acetyl-CoA to ethanol, while the reverse reaction is not impacted by the disruption of the ultrastructures (Kim et al., 2019; Pony et al., 2020; Espinosa et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Prior structural studies on E. coli AdhE captured both the extended and compact forms of the spirosome.
source: Prior structural studies on the E. coli AdhE complex captured both the extended and compact forms of the spirosome, with some biochemical evidence that the extended form was required for the reduction of acetyl-CoA to ethanol (Kim et al., 2019; Pony et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: C. thermocellum AdhE and E. coli AdhE have 62% sequence identity.
source: Because C. thermocellum AdhE and E. coli AdhE have 62% sequence identity, we first aimed to determine the similarity between the AdhE from C. thermocellum and E. coli.
evidence: This is stated as a result from sequence comparison analysis.

claim: The native state of the C. thermocellum spirosome is extended.
source: We determined that the native state of the C. thermocellum spirosome is extended (different from that of other structurally characterized AdhEs) and contains an enclosed channel between the ALDH and ADH active sites.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the structural analysis presented in the study.

claim: The C. thermocellum spirosome contains an enclosed channel between the ALDH and ADH active sites.
source: We determined that the native state of the C. thermocellum spirosome is extended (different from that of other structurally characterized AdhEs) and contains an enclosed channel between the ALDH and ADH active sites.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the structural analysis presented in the study.

claim: The compact spirosome channel leaks acetaldehyde to the bulk phase.
source: In modeling the compact spirosome, we found that this channel leaks acetaldehyde to the bulk phase, which indicates that the extended spirosome might be crucial for toxic aldehyde intermediate channeling.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from MD simulations of the compact spirosome.

claim: The extended spirosome might be crucial for toxic aldehyde intermediate channeling.
source: In modeling the compact spirosome, we found that this channel leaks acetaldehyde to the bulk phase, which indicates that the extended spirosome might be crucial for toxic aldehyde intermediate channeling.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the MD simulation results.

claim: Spirosomes maintained the same conformation between endogenous and exogenous expression in C. thermocellum.
source: Based on negative stain transmission electron microscopy (TEM) data shown in Figure 1A, we found that spirosomes maintained the same conformation between endogenous and exogenous expression – both primarily extended in the case of C. thermocellum, which represents the majority apo conformation of the C. thermocellum spirosome.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from negative stain TEM experiments, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The extended conformation of the C. thermocellum spirosome remained unchanged when purified from E. coli.
source: Intriguingly, the extended conformation of the C. thermocellum spirosome remained unchanged when purified from E. coli, even though the native apo E. coli AdhE is purified primarily in the compact form (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from negative stain TEM experiments, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The native apo E. coli AdhE is purified primarily in the compact form.
source: Intriguingly, the extended conformation of the C. thermocellum spirosome remained unchanged when purified from E. coli, even though the native apo E. coli AdhE is purified primarily in the compact form (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated as an established observation, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Kessler et al. found that the addition of both NAD+ and FeSO4 was necessary to transform E. coli spirosomes from their compact to their extended forms.
source: Since Kessler et al. found that the addition of both NAD+ and FeSO4 was necessary to transform E. coli spirosomes from their compact to their extended forms, we investigated the effects of different reactants that could contribute to the inverse process in the purified, extended C. thermocellum spirosome (Kessler et al., 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The addition of forward reactants (NADH, acetyl-CoA, FeSO4) led to the compaction of C. thermocellum spirosomes.
source: While our results were not as extreme as those of Kessler et al., we found that the addition of the forward reactants (NADH, acetyl-CoA, FeSO4) led to the compaction of spirosomes.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments described in the study.

claim: The addition of reverse reactants (NAD+, ethanol, CoA, FeSO4) to compact E. coli spirosomes resulted in more extended forms.
source: Conversely, the addition of the reverse reactants (NAD+, ethanol, CoA, FeSO4) to the compact E. coli spirosomes resulted in more extended forms.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments described in the study.

claim: NADH and NAD+ were the major determining factors in the conformation of the spirosome.
source: To isolate which substrate was causing this shift, we made negative stained grids of the C. thermocellum spirosomes in the presence of each reactant and found that NADH and NAD+ were the major determining factors in the conformation of the spirosome (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from negative stain experiments, with reference to Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression host does not impact the conformation of the spirosomes but does significantly affect their length.
source: We also found that the expression host does not impact the conformation of the spirosomes but does significantly affect their length (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: C. thermocellum AdhE expressed in E. coli formed spirosomes that were, on average, approximately 20 nm shorter than those found in a native C. thermocellum lysate.
source: C. thermocellum AdhE expressed in E. coli formed spirosomes that were, on average, approximately 20 nm shorter than those found in a native C. thermocellum lysate.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from the length measurements.

claim: The shorter average length of spirosomes in exogenous expression was due largely to the lack of spirosomes longer than 100 nm.
source: This equates to spirosomes that contain, on average, approximately five to ten fewer AdhE monomers in the extended spirosome. The shorter average length was due largely to the lack of spirosomes that were longer than 100 nm in the exogenous expression (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the observed length difference, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Exogenous expression of Vibrio cholerae spirosomes in E. coli resulted in shorter spirosomes.
source: This phenomenon has been observed previously with the exogenous expression of Vibrio cholerae spirosomes in E. coli, which also resulted in shorter spirosomes (Cho et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The dimer interface in C. thermocellum AdhE is a domain-swapped structure where one ALDH domain is sandwiched between the ADH and ALDH domains of the second protein.
source: The first is the buried area located between two molecules of AdhE, in a domain-swapped dimer interface, where one ALDH domain is sandwiched between the ADH and ALDH domains of the second protein.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the structural features observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The tetramer interface occurs only between two ADH domains.
source: The second interface is between the dimer of dimers, here referred to as the tetramer interface. This interface has a much smaller interaction area because it only occurs between two ADH domains (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the structural features observed in the cryo-EM structure, with reference to Figure 2G.

claim: The overall hydrophobicity and electrostatics of the dimer and tetramer interfaces are similar between the C. thermocellum extended, E. coli extended, and E. coli compact structures.
source: Intriguingly, the overall hydrophobicity and electrostatics of these interfaces are similar between the C. thermocellum extended, E. coli extended, and E. coli compact structures (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from comparative structural analysis, with reference to Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The calculated buried surface area differs between the two E. coli dimer interfaces, but not the tetramer interface.
source: However, the calculated buried surface area differs between the two E. coli dimer interfaces, but not the tetramer interface.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from structural analysis.

claim: Both the E. coli and C. thermocellum extended dimer interfaces bury ~5000 Å2.
source: Both the E. coli and C. thermocellum extended dimer interfaces bury ~5000 Å2.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from structural analysis.

claim: The C. thermocellum compact dimer interface buries ~4800 Å2.
source: While the C. thermocellum compact dimer interface buries a similar surface area of ~4800 Å2, the E. coli compact dimer interface buries ~3800 Å2.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from structural analysis.

claim: The E. coli compact dimer interface buries ~3800 Å2.
source: While the C. thermocellum compact dimer interface buries a similar surface area of ~4800 Å2, the E. coli compact dimer interface buries ~3800 Å2.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from structural analysis.

claim: All the tetramer interfaces bury ~2000 Å2.
source: Conversely, all the tetramer interfaces bury ~2000 Å2.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from structural analysis.

claim: More salt bridges form in the extended C. thermocellum structure compared to the extended E. coli structure.
source: We found that more salt bridges form in the extended C. thermocellum structure as compared to the extended E. coli structure, which suggests that this may be a factor in the stability of the extended C. thermocellum structure that is not found in the E. coli structure.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from structural analysis, with an inference about stability.

claim: The E. coli extended structure has two more salt bridges than the compact structure.
source: However, when looking between the E. coli extended and compact structures, there are two more salt bridges in the extended structure than in the compact structure, which again implies that there might be additional factors impacting the primary form of the spirosome (Kim et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from structural analysis, with citations to prior literature.

claim: The extended C. thermocellum spirosome has 44 unique hydrogen bond pairs.
source: When looking at the hydrogen bonds between molecules, the extended C. thermocellum spirosome has a wider variety of hydrogen bonds (44 unique pairs) than the extended E. coli spirosome (32 unique pairs), indicating a potentially more stable structure.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from structural analysis.

claim: The extended E. coli spirosome has 32 unique hydrogen bond pairs.
source: When looking at the hydrogen bonds between molecules, the extended C. thermocellum spirosome has a wider variety of hydrogen bonds (44 unique pairs) than the extended E. coli spirosome (32 unique pairs), indicating a potentially more stable structure.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from structural analysis.

claim: The compact E. coli spirosome has 17 unique hydrogen bond pairs.
source: However, as with the salt bridges, the compact E. coli spirosome has fewer hydrogen bonds (17 unique pairs) than the extended structure, which does not explain why the compact form is the primary structure isolated when purified without substrates.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from structural analysis.

claim: In C. thermocellum, F670 of E. coli is replaced by a tyrosine.
source: In C. thermocellum, F670 is a tyrosine; however, the hydrophobic pocket that surrounds that residue still exists (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from sequence and structural comparison, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The similar shape of tyrosine maintains the integrity of the F670 interaction in C. thermocellum, resulting in stable spirosomes.
source: We postulate that the similar shape of tyrosine maintains the integrity of this interaction, resulting in stable spirosomes.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on structural observations.

claim: The 446-449 deletion in E. coli occurs in the linker between the two domains of the AdhE monomer.
source: Regarding the 446–449 deletion, it occurs in the linker between the two domains of the AdhE monomer.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the location of the deletion.

claim: The linker between the two domains is vital for the domain-swapped structure of the dimer.
source: This linker is vital for the domain-swapped structure of the dimer. Thus, deleting four residues, regardless of the identity of those amino acids, should interfere with the dimerization of AdhE (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from structural analysis, with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Cho et al. found that mutating Y669 and N704 to phenylalanine and serine in V. cholerae AdhE resulted in longer spirosomes.
source: Finally, in V. cholerae AdhE expressed in E. coli (PDBID 7DAG), Cho et al. found that mutating Y669 and N704 to the corresponding residues in E. coli, phenylalanine and serine, resulted in longer spirosomes (i.e. more AdhE subunits in the spirosome) (Cho et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The C. thermocellum sequence aligns with V. cholerae, with a tyrosine and asparagine at positions corresponding to Y669 and N704.
source: The C. thermocellum sequence aligns with V. cholerae, with a tyrosine and asparagine in these positions (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from sequence alignment, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: C. thermocellum AdhE spirosomes, when expressed in E. coli, are significantly shorter than when in their native host.
source: However, based on our negative-stain results (Figure 1C), we show that C. thermocellum AdhE spirosomes, when expressed in E. coli, are significantly shorter than when in their native host.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from negative stain experiments, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Both the ALDH and ADH NAD-pockets are relatively well conserved among 25 AdhE proteins identified in bacteria.
source: In a sequence comparison between 25 AdhE proteins that have been previously identified in bacteria, both the ALDH and ADH NAD-pockets seem relatively well conserved (Figure 5C; Kessler et al., 1992; Matayoshi and Oda, 1985; Extance et al., 2013; Extance et al., 2016; Laurenceau et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from sequence comparison, with reference to Figure 5C and citations to prior literature.

claim: Mutating D494 to glycine results in a change of cofactor preference from NADH to also include NADPH.
source: Using this larger set of sequences, we also analyzed the D494 position. Prior work has shown that mutating the aspartate to glycine results in a change of cofactor preference from NADH to also include NADPH (Tian et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: 2.7% of AdhE sequences had a naturally occurring glycine at the D494 position.
source: There were 2.7% of AdhE sequences that had a naturally occurring G at this position, which suggests that there are AdhE proteins that rely on NADPH for their catalysis.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from sequence analysis.

claim: A potentially novel NAD(P)H binding site was identified at residues 426-431 containing a conserved GxGxxG motif.
source: We were able to visualize a potentially novel NAD(P)H binding site previously only identified via sequence comparison (Figure 5D; Zheng et al., 2015). The sequences contained a conserved GxGxxG motif at residues 426–431, which has been shown to be involved in nucleotide binding (Bellamacina, 1996).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from structural analysis, with reference to Figure 5D and citations to prior literature.

claim: The GxGxxG motif is located at the interface of two AdhE monomers.
source: Intriguingly, this site does not coincide with either the ALD or ALDH active sites and is therefore less likely to have a catalytic function. However, this motif is located at the interface of two AdhE monomers, indicating that it could have an allosteric role, although further studies are needed to confirm.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from structural analysis, with speculation about function.

claim: The three glycines in the GxGxxG motif are all over 99% conserved.
source: The three glycines at this position are all over 99% conserved, indicating that they play an important role in the AdhE structure or function.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from sequence analysis.

claim: The dehydrogenase reaction occurs stepwise to include both NAD+ and acetyl-CoA.
source: We observed that the proteins aligned with very little deviation – less than 2 Å RMSD – causing the acetyl-CoA aligned from R. palustris to sit in most of the same pocket that the NAD+ occupies as aligned from E. coli. This suggests that the dehydrogenase reaction occurs stepwise to include both the NAD+ and the acetyl-CoA (Figure 5G; Zarzycki et al., 2017; Lei et al., 2008; Rudolph et al., 1968).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from structural alignment, with reference to Figure 5G and citations to prior literature.

claim: The NAD+ clashes with the C. thermocellum protein, indicating that the pocket might shift to accommodate NADH separate from acetyl-CoA.
source: Furthermore, when looking at the surface representation of the C. thermocellum structure, we found that the NAD+ clashes with the protein, indicating that the pocket might shift to accommodate NADH separate from acetyl-CoA (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from structural analysis, with reference to Figure 5G.

claim: An empty density was observed at the ADH active site in the C. thermocellum extended structure, coordinated between H734, D844, and C846.
source: At the ADH active site, we observe an empty density in the C. thermocellum extended structure, coordinated between residues that have been implicated in the ADH activity of the protein (Figure 5H, circled in red) (Olson et al., 2023). As illustrated in Figure 5F, we see that there is density, most probably a water molecule, being coordinated by H734, D844, and C846.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from structural analysis, with reference to Figure 5H and a citation to prior literature.

claim: D844 and C846 are 100% conserved among 25 AdhE sequences analyzed.
source: D844 and C846 are 100% conserved, while H734 is 92% conserved among the 25 sequences that we analyzed.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from sequence analysis.

claim: H734 is 92% conserved among 25 AdhE sequences analyzed.
source: D844 and C846 are 100% conserved, while H734 is 92% conserved among the 25 sequences that we analyzed.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from sequence analysis.

claim: MD trajectories demonstrate hydrogen bonding of at least one water molecule with D844 in essentially every frame (>98%).
source: Further supporting our hypothesis that a water molecule may occupy the observed empty density at the ADH active site in the C. thermocellum extended structure, two independent MD trajectories, each with two full AdhE molecules including two ADH active sites, demonstrate hydrogen bonding of at least one water molecule with D844 in essentially every frame (>98%), as well as with H734 (16–31% of the frames) and with C846 (7–66% of frames with both side chain and main chain, as shown in Figure 5I).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from MD simulations, with reference to Figure 5I.

claim: Intermediate channeling has been proposed previously in the E. coli spirosome based on the observation of enclosed space within the structure.
source: Intermediate channeling has been proposed previously in the E. coli spirosome, based on the observation of enclosed space within the structure, and has been hypothesized as a functional role to contain reactive aldehydes and therefore limit cytotoxicity (Pony et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: MOLE 2.0 identified a channel connecting the ALDH and ADH active sites in all three structures (E. coli compact, E. coli extended, and C. thermocellum extended).
source: In all three structures (E. coli compact, E. coli extended, and C. thermocellum extended), as well as a SwissPDB model of the C. thermocellum compact structure, MOLE 2.0 identified a channel that could connect the two active sites.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from computational channel prediction analysis.

claim: The residues lining the extended channel have 92% homology.
source: Overall, the channels are more highly conserved than the overall protein: the residues lining the extended channel have 92% homology, and the residues in the compact channel have 97% homology, whereas the overall protein homology is only 62%.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from sequence analysis.

claim: The residues in the compact channel have 97% homology.
source: Overall, the channels are more highly conserved than the overall protein: the residues lining the extended channel have 92% homology, and the residues in the compact channel have 97% homology, whereas the overall protein homology is only 62%.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from sequence analysis.

claim: There is only one lysine in the tunnel in all three structures.
source: First, there is only one lysine in the tunnel in all three structures, showing one of the largest log2-fold changes as compared to the composition of the full protein (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from structural analysis, with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: The channel may be designed to contain reactive aldehydes while avoiding cross-linking with the amine group of lysine.
source: This may indicate that the channel is designed to contain reactive aldehydes while avoiding cross-linking with the amine group of the lysine.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the structural observation.

claim: There is a higher concentration of histidines in the channel in all structures compared to the full protein.
source: Second, there is a higher concentration of histidines in the channel in all the structures as compared to the full protein. This is potentially due to the tunnel passing by the catalytic iron in the ALDH domain, which is coordinated by three histidines.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from structural analysis, with an inference about the reason.

claim: The extended structures contain a much higher density of phenylalanines in the channel compared to the compact structures.
source: Notably, there is a difference in the number of phenylalanines in the channel when compared between the compact and extended structures. The extended structures contain a much higher density of phenylalanines as indicated by the log2-fold change.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from structural analysis.

claim: In the compact state, only the catalytic cysteine from the ALDH domain is present in the channel.
source: Finally, we focused on the cysteines present in these channels. In the compact state, only the catalytic cysteine from the ALDH domain is present in the channel.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from structural analysis.

claim: In both extended structures, there are two cysteines in the channel: the catalytic cysteine from the ALDH domain and the cysteine in the catalytic pocket from the ADH domain.
source: However, in both extended structures, there are two cysteines in the channel: the catalytic cysteine from the ALDH domain and the cysteine in the catalytic pocket from the ADH domain.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from structural analysis.

claim: The extended spirosome might be the relevant catalytic form because there is a potential path that efficiently connects the active sites.
source: This could point to the extended spirosome as being the relevant catalytic form because there is a potential path that efficiently connects the active sites.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the structural observations.

claim: The residence time for acetaldehyde when the spirosome is in the extended conformation is significantly longer than the compact conformation.
source: The primary conclusion from these is that the residence time for acetaldehyde when the spirosome is in the extended conformation is significantly longer than the compact conformation (Figure 7E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from MD simulations, with reference to Figure 7E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The trajectory of the aldehyde tracks quite closely with the channel found by MOLE.
source: In addition, the trajectory of the aldehyde tracks quite closely with the channel found by MOLE (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from MD simulations, with reference to Figure 7A and B.

claim: Simulations initiated with the spirosome in the compact conformation typically see acetaldehyde leave within 4 ns (ALDH active site starting position) to 30 ns (starting point midway in the channel).
source: In contrast, simulations initiated with the spirosome in the compact conformation typically see acetaldehyde leave within 4 ns (ALDH active site starting position) to 30 ns (starting point midway in the channel).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from MD simulations.

claim: The basic conclusions from E. coli AdhE MD simulations are analogous to the C. thermocellum AdhE simulations.
source: We conducted analogous simulations with the E. coli AdhE and found the basic conclusions to be analogous to the C. thermocellum AdhE (Figure 7, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from MD simulations, with reference to Figure 7 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: CryoDRGN analysis indicated the existence of at least four distinct spirosome conformations.
source: Correlation between particles visualized graphically in the Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) (Figure 8A) indicated the existence of at least four distinct spirosome conformations.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from cryoDRGN analysis, with reference to Figure 8A.

claim: Volumes generated from particle subgroups indicated the presence of extended, compact, and at least two major intermediate conformations.
source: Volumes generated from these particle subgroups indicated the presence of extended, compact, and at least two major intermediate conformations (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from cryoDRGN analysis, with reference to Figure 8B.

claim: 6.7% of picked particles were compact spirosomes.
source: These templates were then used as a visual reference, which did indeed reveal the presence of compact 2D projections within the C. thermocellum cryo-EM data (6.7% of picked particles were compact) that were previously overlooked (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from cryo-EM data analysis, with reference to Figure 8D.

claim: A 3.93 Å density of the compact AdhE spirosome was obtained.
source: The subsequent reconstruction using these particles yielded a 3.93 Å density of the compact AdhE spirosome, although there was evidence of streaking due to preferred orientation issues and low particle numbers.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: The C. thermocellum AdhE does not achieve as compact a state as previously reported compact AdhE spirosomes from different species.
source: There are some intriguing insights into differences between our compact ultrastructure compared to previously reported compact AdhE spirosomes isolated from different species (Kim et al., 2019; Pony et al., 2020; Cho et al., 2021). Most notably, the C. thermocellum AdhE does not achieve as compact a state, even when isolating the most compact particles.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from structural comparison, with citations to prior literature.

claim: Compact spirosomes observed via negative staining are also present in near-native conditions (cryogenically preserved samples).
source: Moreover, the reconstruction of a compact spirosome density corroborates that compact spirosomes observed via negative staining are also present in near-native conditions (cryogenically preserved samples).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from comparing negative stain and cryo-EM data.

claim: Spirosomes have the potential to exist in a spectrum of states that can be captured in a single cryo-EM grid without any additional cofactors.
source: This data confirms that spirosomes have the potential to exist in a spectrum of states that can be captured in a single cryo-EM grid without any additional cofactors to induce conformational changes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the cryo-EM data analysis.

claim: The extended conformation is the more structurally stable form in both E. coli and C. thermocellum.
source: Our structural comparison identifies the extended conformation as the more structurally stable form in both the case of E. coli and C. thermocellum, which disagrees with the reality of the compact spirosome being the stable, apo conformation from E. coli.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from structural analysis.

claim: Extended spirosomes have a larger buried surface area in the dimer interface than compact spirosomes (5000 Å2 compared to 3800 Å2).
source: Furthermore, extended spirosomes have a larger buried surface area in the dimer interface than the compact spirosomes (5000 Å2 compared to 3800 Å2, respectively), imparting additional stability.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from structural analysis, with an inference about stability.

claim: Conformation does not rely solely upon the environment; C. thermocellum spirosomes are extended in both endogenous and exogenous expression conditions.
source: Although we could not structurally identify exact features that would predict which conformation was preferred, we have evidence from negative-stain EM experiments that conformation does not rely solely upon the environment: C. thermocellum spirosomes are extended in both endogenous and exogenous expression conditions.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from negative stain EM experiments.

claim: Compact spirosomes have only been isolated from Gram-negatives while solely extended spirosomes have been isolated from Gram-positives.
source: This could potentially be due to the differences between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. In previous studies, compact spirosomes have only been isolated from Gram-negatives while solely extended spirosomes have been isolated from Gram-positives.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from prior studies, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Compact spirosomes can transition to extended in the presence of cofactors, but the reverse has not been previously observed with an extended spirosome.
source: Furthermore, while the compact spirosomes can transition to extended in the presence of cofactors, the reverse has not been previously observed with an extended spirosome (Matayoshi and Oda, 1985; Kim et al., 2019; Pony et al., 2020; Laurenceau et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Compact spirosomes were identified in a native C. thermocellum lysate.
source: While these compact spirosomes could result from expression in E. coli, we also identified compact spirosomes in a native C. thermocellum lysate, which would not have similar contamination issues.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from experiments with native C. thermocellum.

claim: A potential novel allosteric NAD(P)H binding site lies between two monomers of AdhE, identified by a characteristic NAD(P)H binding motif.
source: Close examination of the structure revealed a potential novel allosteric NAD(P)H binding site that lies between two monomers of AdhE, identified by a characteristic NAD(P)H binding motif.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from structural analysis.

claim: The spirosome is necessary for the acetyl-CoA to acetaldehyde reaction in the ALDH domain, yet unneeded for the reverse reaction or for ADH activity.
source: An intriguing finding from prior research is that the spirosome is necessary for the acetyl-CoA to acetaldehyde reaction in the ALDH domain, yet unneeded for the reverse reaction or for ADH activity (Kim et al., 2019; Pony et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A channel might be necessary to funnel acetaldehyde away from the ALDH active site to prevent product inhibition.
source: Therefore, a channel might be necessary to funnel acetaldehyde away from the ALDH active site to prevent product inhibition in the ALDH site.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on prior findings.

claim: The channel in the compact conformation has areas that are exposed to the cytosol, whereas the extended channel is entirely enclosed.
source: Here, we identified an enclosed tunnel between an ALDH domain and an ADH domain of two separate proteins in C. thermocellum and used MD to examine possible aldehyde channeling. While the channel can be found in both the compact and extended structures, we see that the channel in the compact conformation has areas that are exposed to the cytosol, whereas the extended channel is entirely enclosed.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from structural and MD analysis.

claim: The extended spirosome is the active form of AdhE.
source: This further supports the idea that the extended spirosome is the active form of AdhE (Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the structural observations, with a citation to prior literature.

claim: MD simulations show that the aldehyde intermediate has a much longer occupation time in the channel of the extended form.
source: MD simulations further corroborate this, showing that the aldehyde intermediate has a much longer occupation time in the channel of the extended form.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from MD simulations.
